cells.tense: The ending already happened, and you're standing where it left off, deciding what to put there next.
cells.ask: Give one thing that's grown into the cleared room a day this week — a class, a call, a morning you keep for yourself. See what putting a date on it does to how the room feels.
cells.core:
The ending already happened because what was in your hands finished, and you let it finish. There's no score to settle with it and no lid to keep on it. You're in the space the ending opened, and you're in it with your eyes up, which is what makes it usable.

What the ending left behind is room, and room is something you can tend. Part of what you released made way for something still small — a habit, a person, a direction — and small things grow on steady care, not on force. Give one of them a slot on the calendar and see whether it holds when nothing is pushing it.
cells.sheetLine: The ending's done, and what's here now is room you get to fill.
cells.verb: letting go of what no longer fits, on purpose, before it's taken from you
cells.place: the open ground after something has ended and before the next thing has started

cells.tense: You're already dropping things that haven't asked to be let go of, clearing for a loss that hasn't arrived.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're still keeping and give it a fixed ten minutes a day for two weeks — same slot, no more, no less. What the practice returns to you, not to anyone else, is the useful part.
cells.core:
You're surrendering ahead of the surrender. Things get dropped before they're finished, conversations get abandoned before they've been had, and you can call it moving on, but it's really moving first — getting the loss over with before it can pick its own timing. What that protects isn't obvious from inside it.

When this works, the release is quiet and it waits for the thing to actually be over. Until then, the practice is to stay with one thing on purpose: same slot, same attention, small and repeated, kept lit by your own hand. That steadiness is what tells the difference between releasing and bracing.
cells.sheetLine: You're ending things before they've ended, and calling it release.

cells.tense: Something is over and you're still in the room with your hands full, holding what the ending would take if you let it.
cells.ask: Write one sentence on paper: what this grip keeps you from doing, and one thing you'd be free to do without it, without saying yet whether you'll let the thing go. Then keep the paper.
cells.core:
You can hold a lot, and you have. The hands are full in ways that show in small places — the flat tone when the subject comes up, the way you check whether it's really finished. Nothing is actually being held up by it; it's just being held, which is a different kind of weight.

Holding well includes being able to set something down when holding it no longer serves what you're holding it for. Pick one thing and put into a sentence what the grip keeps you from and what you'd do without it. You don't have to release it today. But the sentence is the start of knowing what you're choosing, and the hand that writes it is the hand that can open.
cells.sheetLine: You're holding something up that doesn't need holding anymore.

cells.tense: Something here has already been released — or hasn't — and the story you tell about it says otherwise either way.
cells.ask: Take five minutes and write two lists on one sheet: what's already been let go of, and what's still being held. Set a timer and write both without editing.
cells.core:
Something got put down and you still describe it as ongoing. Or something is still in your hands and you describe it as already gone. Either way the facts on the ground and the story in your mouth have drifted apart, and only one of them is doing the steering.

The honest version is gentler than it sounds. When this is working, the story matches the ground: what's finished is spoken of as finished, what's still held is owned as held, and the two lists don't need to agree with each other. Five minutes, one sheet, two lists — what's done with, and what isn't. Care can go to what's still growing once the ledger is straight, and the ledger is a piece of paper, not a verdict.

attempts.check: The record establishes only a capacity and a seat: willing release seated in necessary endings. Any sentence that says what this person has been holding, how long, or who was involved would be invention, so the cells locate the grip and stop. The reader could reasonably say the ending in question is not theirs to choose — a decision still pending, a situation that may yet resolve — so the ask is written small and does not require the ending to be real: writing down what no longer fits is useful even if the ending is wrong, because it shows where the grip lives. The sentence that serves the writer most is any about 'clearing space' as a poetic fact; the person needs the specific next action, not the poetry, so the poetry stays out.
